item.title: Wall Street on track for record profits
item.description:
Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation.

Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report.

Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading.

By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026.

  • If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion.

Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says.

Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025.

Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering.

  • Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers.

Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first.

  • There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them.

The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines.

  • Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading.

What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines.

  • Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading.

What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

item.title: Latino group bets on bilingual AI to cut voter confusion before the midterms
item.description:
A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish.

Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs.

  • Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center.
  • The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll.

How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information.

  • Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration.
  • Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level.

Unlike a general-purpose chatbot, Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers.

  • The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer.
  • If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response.

State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology.

  • The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version.
  • Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment."
  • The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change.

Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation.

  • A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist.
  • Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer.
  • The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place.

What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place.

  • He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes.
  • Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach.

Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections.

  • Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006.
  • Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party.
  • In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.

item.title: Scoop: Gun safety groups jump into midterms with $10 million assist for Democrats
item.description:
Everytown for Gun Safety, a group that advocates for stricter gun laws, is teaming up with House Democrats on a $10 million ad campaign to boost former gun safety advocates now running for Congress, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: That's a significant sum at a moment when Democrats are raising alarm bells about being outgunned financially in the midterm elections.

  • The candidates boosted by the campaign are all former volunteers for Moms Demand Action, which is part of Everytown.
  • The candidates include: JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Pia Dandiya of Florida, Christina Bohannan, Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James of Iowa, Christina Hines and Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, and Paige Cognetti of Pennsylvania.

"For nearly two years, a MAGA House has rubber-stamped the Trump administration as it tore up federal gun safety laws, and flipping these eight seats is how we put a stop to it," Everytown president John Feinblatt said in a statement first shared with Axios.

  • "There's a Moms Demand Action volunteer on the ballot in every one of these districts, and we're partnering with House Majority PAC to turn them into majority makers."
  • Mike Smith, the president of House Democrats' main super PAC, House Majority PAC, said in a statement: "Every seat on this map is a chance to put a check on a Trump administration and a MAGA House that have spent two years putting the gun lobby ahead of American families."

Between the lines: The money will go to fund TV and digital ads focused broadly on "public safety," referencing not just gun control but drug trafficking, immigration, crime, and police funding.

  • The Bohannan ad says she is "running for Congress to put public safety first. That means working with both parties to secure our border, hire more police officers and keep illegal guns and fentanyl off our streets."
  • The Cognetti ad mostly focuses on her broader anti-corruption message but lauds how "she got millions for police and cut violent crime by 80%" as mayor of Scranton.

The other side: "House Democrats have fully embraced the radical socialist agenda of abolishing prisons, releasing criminals back on the streets, and defunding the police," NRCC spokesman Mike Marinella told Axios in a statement.

  • "Voters won't buy their lies about Republicans who have fought to protect our communities."

Editor's note: This article has been corrected to clarify that Moms Demand Action is part of Everytown.

item.title: Inside Trump's new AI playbook
item.description:
President Trump's newly minted "super intelligence" task force faces a daunting mandate: Reconcile fiercely divided Cabinet factions to create a tech policy that keeps pace with the blistering AI race.

Why it matters: The task force brings the administration's scattered AI work under one roof, but it also makes it likely that any new rules will be forged in the crossfire of competing internal camps.

  • In an interview, task force co-chair Scott Kupor rejected the assertion that the administration is asleep at the wheel on AI policy, arguing that rigid, static legislation would risk becoming instantly obsolete.

What they're saying: "The worst thing for us to do would be to assume a static set of knowledge that allows us to put a regulatory schema in place that then has unintended consequences," said Kupor, a Silicon Valley veteran who is currently serving as director of the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, akin to an HR director for the federal government.

  • "Look, we live in D.C.," he said. "There's nothing that's not political in this town. People have different views and that's totally fine. Our obligation is to demonstrate to the American people that this is good and also that we take the anxieties and the concerns seriously."
  • "At the end of the day there is no daylight between the president and anyone else ... we need to win," he said.

Between the lines: The group's makeup highlights the competing fiefdoms driving Trump's AI strategy, with some working on model approval and coordination and others continuing to voice deep skepticism about pro-regulation forces in the industry.

  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trump Chief of Staff Susie Wiles have worked behind the scenes to encourage some oversight, including through the voluntary model-review process that already exists.
  • Managed within the Commerce Department, the reviews have already been used for top models at Anthropic, OpenAI and now Google, sources tell Axios.
  • On the other end of the spectrum, figures like David Sacks and the Pentagon's Emil Michael represent an approach that is wary of the potential for a slowdown in model development or new regulation to reduce competition for frontier companies.
  • Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence and the new AI czar, is expected to bring cohesion to the group's collective work, much as he does with the myriad intelligence agencies.

The entire committee is set to operate under Trump's explicit marching orders: Innovation cannot be bottlenecked, and America must stay ahead while finding a safe path forward, Kupor said.

  • Kupor suggested one outcome may be that AI regulation is divided among different federal agencies, although it is too early to know what the group — which will do its work over 120 days — will ultimately recommend to the president.
  • His primary area of focus initially will be to seek input from stakeholders in the energy, manufacturing, security and financial services industries. Kupor said he expects Clayton will keep close tabs on the intelligence community and the committee will continue to stay in close touch with the AI companies.

Zoom in: The administration is leaning hard into corporate self-policing to manage the risks. Kupor and other officials believe that third-party audits and direct reporting to corporate boards carry severe securities law implications that rival traditional government oversight.

The bottom line: The task force's goal isn't to draft a bureaucratic "Ph.D. dissertation," in Kupor's words. But it remains to be seen whether streamlining existing efforts without new legislation will satisfy Americans who are increasingly anxious about AI safety.

item.title: The most-watched election in U.S. history
item.description:
The 2026 midterms are shaping up to be the most intensely observed, recorded, dissected and challenged election in American history.

Why it matters: A small army of partisan and nonpartisan observers will show up. So will a surge of Justice Department monitors, organizers looking for signs of ICE and citizen journalists broadcasting their search for illegal voting in real time.

Between the lines: More nonpartisan observation can bolster confidence in elections, studies show. But officials worry that activists expecting to find wrongdoing could misread routine events.

  • Election officials have been raising concerns that "vigilante citizen journalists" could interfere with the election, said Andrew Walchuck of Common Cause, a nonprofit organization that's also recruiting nonpartisan election observers.
  • "I worry that people are going to go in and claim they're seeing things that they aren't," said Andrew Garber of the Brennan Center.
  • "Just minor, innocuous things that are going to happen as millions and millions of ballots get cast and counted, then it gets spun into something nefarious or untrue," Garber said.

The intrigue: After the 2020 election, claims from observers and activist sleuths helped fuel challenges to the results.

  • It was then channeled into numerous lawsuits from the Trump campaign. The cases were almost all dismissed or denied relief in court.

Influencers and online activists can turn real-time claims about wrongdoing into national controversy before officials can weigh in or push back — including while votes are being cast or counted.

  • "What gives me concern is that we have an administration that is trying to spread conspiracy theories and spread lies about our elections and... [then] having more people out there with that purpose behind their work troubles me," Walchuck said.

The other side: "Despite extreme Democrats and the media claiming it never happens, the evidence of voter fraud continues to pile up. Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable," Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman, said in a statement.

  • This year there have been more than two dozen federal charges against people for voting when they're not eligible and about 160 arrests, according to the Justice Department.
  • A review from the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonpartisan organization, says instances of illegal voting are "extremely small."

Zoom in: The DOJ plans to train 1,000 election monitors to deploy across the country, one of the largest-ever efforts from the agency. It builds on a significant increase in observers in 2024.

  • The Senate Democrats have spun up their own arm of election observers, using office staff to monitor the polls. That's in addition to a new 50-state-plus-territories recruitment program by a coalition of Democratic state parties, aiming to recruit at least 10,000 election watchers.
  • The Republican National Committee is building on its election watch network set up in 2020 to counter perceived voter fraud. GOP partisans have signed up in record numbers to be poll workers and the party is hosting virtual and in-person trainings for observers and challengers.
  • A network of anti-ICE activists is transitioning ICE watch trainings into poll watching trainings, responding in part to the Trump administration saying ICE could make arrests at the polls. When asked in September about deploying agents, Trump told TIME magazine he hadn't thought of it.

Zoom out: These efforts will coexist with a slew of nonpartisan observing efforts, ranging from voter protection groups to international election observers.

  • There will also be state party and campaign staffers who regularly monitor the polls for concerns. These are typically more mundane, including monitoring accurate opening and closing times for polling locations that can be remedied with quick litigation.
  • The rules and terminology for observers vary by state laws, which also govern how close an observer can be to voting machines or tabulation processes and how to document concerns about malpractice.

The bottom line: "Having questions and wanting to understand more about the election process as a sort of curious citizen is a good thing," said Avery Davis-Roberts of the Carter Center, which monitors elections internationally and will have volunteers in five states in November.

  • "And we hope that people will use observation and the findings of our observation as a way to better understand how the process works and maybe have some of those questions answered."

item.title: Inside the transgender rights fight injecting chaos into Democrats' midterm efforts
item.description:
An intra-party debate over how best to deflect Republican attacks on transgender issues has Democrats angrily sniping at each other just weeks out from the midterm elections.

Why it matters: This is not the position Democrats hoped to be in two years after their 2024 election loss, which many in the party attributed to being outflanked by GOP messaging on trans issues.

  • "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios.
  • "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance."
  • "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care."

Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools."

  • "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports."
  • Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down.
  • One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community."

What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC.

  • He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us."
  • Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable."

What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios.

  • The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election.
  • "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer.
  • "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor."

Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric.

  • Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls."
  • That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it.

The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024.

  • "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC.
  • Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy."

Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios.

  • "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules."
  • "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care."

The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck.

  • Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue.
  • Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

  • "People feel you need to respond in some way to some of these attacks because people didn't do it two years ago," Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.), a co-chair of the Congressional LGBTQ+ Equality Caucus, told Axios.
  • "But you also need to realize what we're winning on right now," Pocan added, saying Democratic candidates need to strike "a balance."
  • "Silence is deadly, and I think we played that out in 2024," said Lanae Erickson, a senior vice president at the centrist think tank Third Way, citing polling that found most voters believed Democrats "thought there should be no rules in sports, no rules around health care."

Driving the news: Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) set off a firestorm in her district and on Capitol Hill in September by stating in a direct-to-camera ad that she "voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools."

  • "Parents know what's best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls' sports," Kaptur said in the spot — a response to an ad from Republican Derek Merrin that said she "voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports."
  • Multiple county parties condemned the ad — particularly the reference to transgender girls as "boys" — and urged Kaptur to take it down.
  • One LGBTQ+ group, the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, said in a statement there is "no difference" between Kaptur and Merrin because they are "both united against the LBTQIA+ community."

What they're saying: "The ads were deeply offensive to the Equality Caucus and the broader LGBTQ community that we represent," said Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the caucus' political arm, Equality PAC.

  • He told Axios: "The Equality Caucus is not going to stand by passively and allow anyone to scapegoat the trans community. It is a red line for us."
  • Equality PAC "is absolutely not supporting her campaign at this time," the group said in a separate statement to Axios, calling Kaptur's language "unacceptable."

What we're hearing: Kaptur's colleagues also privately communicated their disgust with the ad to her office, multiple House Democrats familiar with the matter told Axios.

  • The lawmakers predicted there will be in-person conversations with Kaptur when the House returns in November, especially if she wins her election.
  • "Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls' sports stay fair," said Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer.
  • "She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor."

Zoom out: It's not just Kaptur. Democratic House candidates Blake Gendebien of New York and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa, and Senate candidate Mary Peltola of Alaska, have put out ads featuring similar rhetoric.

  • Rep. Don Davis (D-N.C.) released an ad last week in which he said there are "real concerns about fairness and safety" and that "states should decide what's right for protecting women and girls."
  • That ad, like Kaptur's, raised eyebrows privately among LGBTQ+ House Democrats, though none have called him out publicly for it.

The other side: Centrist groups and lawmakers say the party has to be realistic about districts like Kaptur's, which President Trump carried by 11 percentage points in 2024.

  • "Marcy Kaptur and Don Davis are doing the most important work in Democratic politics: winning Trump districts," said Liam Kerr, cofounder of centrist group Welcome PAC.
  • Kerr argued attacks from LGBTQ+ groups will only help swing-district Democrats: "Taking the 20% side of an 80/20 issue may be bad politics, but elevating the big winners repudiating you is even worse advocacy."

Between the lines: "Our latest [research] showed that anti-trans attacks take about 8 points off of the Democratic vote if you just let it sit out there," Erickson, the Third Way official, told Axios.

  • "But there are ways to respond that get you back up 10 to 12 to 14 points," she continued. "There are a bunch of different ways to say it ... just being clear that there need to be rules. Not laws, but rules."
  • "When it comes to health care, that parents, not politicians, should be in charge of decisions about their kids' health care."

The bottom line: Centrists and LGBTQ+ Democrats alike say a careful balance can and should be struck.

  • Several lawmakers pointed to Senate hopefuls James Talarico and Sherrod Brown as examples for deftly maneuvering on this issue.
  • Erickson said "calling transgender girls 'boys' ... is not respectful" and that candidates "don't have to do it. There's better ways to talk about this."

item.title: U.S. B-1 bombers evacuated from UK base because of threat of Iranian drone attack
item.description:
The U.S. military evacuated a dozen B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford airbase in the UK over the weekend as a result of intelligence suggesting an Iranian drone attack, U.S. officials said.

Why it matters: Such an Iranian drone attack from British soil against the base could have led to the killing of U.S. service members and destroyed the strategic bombers.

  • It would have been an unprecedented and brazen attack by Iran against a U.S. base in Europe — with the potential for dramatic escalation in the war in the Middle East.
  • When asked by reporters on Monday if Iran planned to launch a drone attack against the base from British soil, Trump said: "I can't tell you that. If they did they will suffer greatly."

Driving the news: The dozen B-1 bombers were evacuated from the base in the UK only several weeks after being deployed there.

  • The Pentagon said on Sunday that "all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States."
  • It added that the U.S. military bomber force, including B-1s, B-2s, and B-52s, "remain ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities — including through operations that launch and recover from the continental United States."

Between the lines: The decision to move the bombers came several days after British security forces arrested several dual British-Iranian citizens suspected of planning an attack on the base.

  • U.S. officials say it is unclear whether the people who were arrested are connected to the alleged planned drone attack or if they were planning a different attack.

Behind the scenes: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel gave the UK intelligence that pointed to a threat of an Iranian attack.

  • On Monday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Netanyahu from the plane on his way to Iceland, the State Department said.

What they're saying: Rubio told reporters earlier that the movement of the bombers was part of "regular rotations" of U.S. Air Force assets around the world and was not directly tied to an Iranian threat.

  • But several hours later, President Trump contradicted Rubio and told reporters the bombers were moved because of a security threat from Iran.
  • "They didn't fly out by accident ... there was a threat. We moved them around a little bit," he said.
  • Trump added that the U.S. knows who was behind the threat and their links to Iran.
  • Trump was then asked about the attempted terrorist attack on the Fly Dubai flight and said he thinks Iran was responsible.

item.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
item.description:
President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague, though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it.

Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began.

Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia.

  • There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution.
  • Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work.
  • No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported.

What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday.

  • "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can."
  • Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger."
  • The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance, but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early

Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert.

  • The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak.

Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

item.title: How states are tackling midterm pump pain
item.description:
States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections, pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled.

Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs.

  • While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution.

Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief.

Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing.

  • There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders.

Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March.

  • Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days.
  • Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months.
  • Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters.

Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so.

  • Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels.
  • But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns.

Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries.

  • For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities."
  • Louisiana, Nebraska, North Carolina, Oklahoma and Texas took similar action.
  • Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring.

The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action.

Go deeper: Iran war drives $100 billion in extra energy costs for U.S. consumers

item.title: GOP senator warns Anthropic of "alarmist" approach to AI
item.description:
Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) is urging Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei against an "alarmist approach" and "panic-inducing commentary" on AI, according to a letter sent Monday and obtained by Axios.

Why it matters: It's the latest example of President Trump's allies targeting Amodei. Moreno's letter comes ahead of Anthropic's expected historic IPO, with valuation estimates as high as nearly $2 trillion.

  • "I do not understand how you can ask them to invest their hard-earned savings in Anthropic's continued development while warning those same Americans that your product could ultimately lead to their extinction," Moreno wrote, referencing the expected IPO.

Zoom in: "With great power comes great responsibility," Moreno wrote, "and in this case, I am concerned that you are failing to meet the moment."

  • Moreno adopted Trump's new terminology, replacing artificial intelligence (AI) with super intelligence (SI).
  • He said Amodei's own words agreeing with "doomer" views about the potential for AI to kill humans, "indicate that your instinct is to wreak havoc on the public SI discourse."
  • Moreno urged more emphasis on how AI can also be used to protect against the very safety threats being warned about as well as how how it can strengthen national security and ensure the U.S. stays ahead of China.

Zoom out: Public concern over AI advancement and data centers has become a focus of the midterm election.

  • Moreno's fellow Ohio Republican, Sen. Jon Husted, has faced an onslaught of ads accusing him of being pro-data centers as he seeks re-election.

item.title: House GOP whip: Limit spending to districts with "biggest return"
item.description:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is scaling back expectations and zeroing in on a narrowed battlefield as Republicans' prospects of keeping their majority look increasingly bleak.

Why it matters: Emmer, a former National Republican Congressional Committee chair who helped the GOP unexpectedly gain seats in 2020, argues his party can still defy historical headwinds in November.

  • But with less than a month to go, Emmer acknowledges that some tough decisions are coming about where Republicans spend their money, including walking away from races they don't think they can salvage.
  • "It really is a business, and you're looking at a balance sheet, and you're putting your money where you're gonna get your biggest return," he told Axios aboard a plane between campaign stops.
  • Axios joined Emmer, who plans to visit 56 districts between September and Election Day, as he traveled from Charlotte to Richmond last week for stops with Reps. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) and Rob Wittman (R-Va.).

Driving the news: It's a lesson Emmer says Republicans learned the hard way in 2022, when expectations of a "red wave" led the party to spread its resources too broadly.

  • "We expanded the map when we should have kept it narrow," Emmer told donors in Charlotte. "We should have been conservative about what we were going after."
  • This cycle, Emmer said Republicans have to identify "where you're not gonna be able to salvage this, and you've got to pick up something over there."

Yes, but: That strategy is being tested by a difficult national environment for Republicans, with an unpopular president and voters focused on the cost of living and the war in Iran, which is driving up gas prices.

Between the lines: Asked about embattled Rep. Max Miller's (R-Ohio) increasingly difficult race, Emmer immediately pointed up the ticket to the Senate and gubernatorial races, where Democrats are faring better than expected.

  • "The problem is, when you got these statewide candidates that are not creating momentum, that's tough," he said.
  • Emmer also pointed to the North Carolina Senate race, where Democrat Roy Cooper has opened up a lead in polls, as having a "large impact" on the 1st and 11th district races there.
  • Miller has a path to victory, Emmer said, "but it's narrow." Still, he defended the NRCC's decision to spend money backing Miller.

Zoom in: Emmer's instinct is to let members run the race that fits their district — within limits.

  • He called Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar's (R-Fla.) campaign ad breaking with Trump on immigration a "huge mistake," adding, "I'm not sure why now was the time for that message" (although he later walked back those comments, saying Salazar "knows her district").
  • Salazar posited in the ad that Trump's immigration enforcement efforts have "gone too far" and that Hispanic voters who helped elect him in 2024 "feel betrayed."

item.title: Eurodrama in currency markets raises U.S. dollar's standing
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

The euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar on Monday as political and fiscal worries rattled European markets.

Why it matters: Rising borrowing costs and political instability are reviving concerns about strains within the eurozone — and whether the European Central Bank may eventually have to step in.

  • France is grappling with high deficits, rising long-term rates and political stalemate over how to address them, as our colleague Emily Peck noted.
  • Spain's prime minister called a snap election for Nov. 29, which could strengthen Pedro Sánchez's position or open the door to a populist right government.

By the numbers: The euro fell below $1.12, its lowest since May 2025 and down about 4% since Sept. 8.

Between the lines: France's rising borrowing costs echo the eurozone crisis of the early 2010s, though the ECB now has more tools to contain market stress.

What they're saying: In an opinion article Monday in the Financial Times, former ECB board member Lorenzo Bini Smaghi called for the central bank to suspend its quantitative tightening program in light of stress on long-term rates.

  • Compared with the early 2010s, the ECB "is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency," he wrote. "It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields."
  • "However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening," he continues, or shrinking its balance sheet by not replacing government bonds as they mature.
  • "This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure," Bini Smaghi wrote.

item.title: Dennis Hastert, disgraced ex-House speaker, dies at 84
item.description:
Dennis Hastert, the longest-serving Republican House speaker in U.S. history who later admitted to sexually abusing several teenage boys, died Saturday at 84.

The big picture: Hastert was the highest-ranking elected official in U.S. history to serve time in federal prison, and Congress still conducts business under an unwritten rule named after him.

Driving the news: Hastert died at his home in Plano, Illinois, while under hospice care, the Kendall County Coroner's Office told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • He is survived by his wife, Jean Kahl, and their two sons.

Catch up quick: Hastert pleaded guilty to evading banking laws in 2015 after prosecutors investigated him for concealing large cash withdrawals.

  • Court proceedings revealed he paid hush money to cover up his past sexual abuse of boys while working as a teacher and high school wrestling coach.
  • Prosecutors alleged that Hastert molested at least four boys, some as young as 14.
  • He faced no sexual abuse charges due to the statute of limitations. He was sentenced to 15 months in prison and released in 2017 after serving 13 months.

Zoom out: While in Congress, Hastert became known for the unwritten Hastert Rule, under which the speaker will only bring a bill to the floor for a vote if a majority of the majority party supports it.

  • Critics say the rule encouraged partisanship by keeping bipartisan bills off the floor if they lack support from most members of the majority party.

Early life

Hastert was born in Aurora, Kane County, Illinois, on Jan. 2, 1942.

  • He attended Wheaton College and earned a master's degree from Northern Illinois University.
  • He later worked as a high school teacher and athletic coach at Yorkville High School, where the abuse of at least four athletes took place.

He left education for politics, winning a seat in the Illinois House of Representatives, where he served from 1980 to 1986.

  • Hastert then won election to the U.S. House, serving from 1987 to 2007.

Professional career

Hastert has been dubbed the "accidental speaker" after he won the gavel in 1999 as a compromise candidate after Newt Gingrich resigned and the expected replacement, Bob Livingston, withdrew.

  • Hastert led the House during the aftermath of the 9/11 terror attacks and for most of President George W. Bush's administration.

After his resignation, he became a highly paid lobbyist until his indictment.

The indictment

Hastert pleaded guilty in 2015 to one count of illegally structuring cash withdrawals to evade federal reporting requirements.

  • His plea agreement says Hastert paid an unnamed individual $1.7 million between 2010 and 2014 after the person confronted him about "past misconduct" Hastert committed against them decades earlier.
  • Hastert had agreed to pay the individual $3.5 million to resolve the matter. From 2010 to 2012, he regularly withdrew roughly $50,000 in cash every six weeks to make the payments.
  • After bank representatives questioned him about the large withdrawals, Hastert began taking out less than $10,000 at a time to evade federal reporting requirements. He ultimately withdrew $952,000 in those smaller increments.
  • Hastert later stopped making payments before reaching the agreed-upon $3.5 million, prompting the individual to sue him for the remaining money. That lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court.

After the indictment

Hastert's state pensions from working as a teacher and in the state legislature were forfeited and revoked in the years after his indictment.

  • His federal pension, worth more than $70,000 a year, was still in place.

His name was also removed from Wheaton University's Center for Economics, Government, and Public Policy in 2015, and his official House Speaker portrait was removed from the Speaker's Lobby.

Go deeper: Former House Speaker Dennis Hastert settles child sexual abuse payments suit

item.title: Trump's economic tightrope messaging of strong economy, high prices
item.description:
President Trump's economic officials acknowledge that a strong economy alone will not persuade Americans that they are better off under this president.

Why it matters: The administration is trying to avoid what it sees as a Biden-era mistake: touting strong economic data while Americans are still reeling from a historic run-up in prices to which Trump's policies have contributed.

  • It is a high-wire messaging act just weeks before the midterms: The administration wants to promote strong growth without appearing to dismiss Americans' frustration over the cost of living.
  • "If I say, 'Oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," top White House economist Kevin Hassett said on CNN's "State of the Union" on Sunday.

What they're saying: "What we're not going to do is do what the Biden people did and tell the American people how good they had it," Bessent told Axios' Mike Allen on Friday in a wide-ranging interview on "The Axios Show."

  • Bessent said that the economy remains strong despite the recent inflation surge. "Any of the numbers are quite strong, other than headline inflation," which includes energy prices driven up by the Middle East conflict. He predicted the energy shock would "fade away."
  • He acknowledged that Americans are still dealing with the cumulative hit from higher prices: "Sometimes I feel like an emergency room doctor. ... The American people were backed over by the inflation Mack Truck."
  • The Treasury secretary said that wages keeping pace with inflation now isn't enough to make up for the earlier erosion in purchasing power. "Breaking even after what happened during the Biden years is not our goal."

Yes, but: The administration still wants credit for the strong economy on paper, even as the headline economic indicators obscure the financial strain Americans still feel.

  • "There is the stated preference and revealed preference," Bessent said, referring to Americans' spending behavior versus their weak sentiment.

The other side: "What we did was to say, 'hey, we know you're struggling and we're trying to help with prices, but look at this good GDP or jobs report!' That talked past people," Jared Bernstein, former White House top economist under Biden, told Axios in an email.

  • "What they mostly say is 'You're not struggling! And the economy's booming.' That too talks past people."
  • Bernstein argued that the administration has not only dismissed affordability concerns — Trump called the affordability crisis a "hoax" last year — but worsened them through tariffs, budget cuts and the war.

The big picture: The bond market is complicating the administration's affordability push as long-term interest rates rise sharply and mortgage rates top 7%.

  • Bessent has made lower Treasury yields a pillar of the administration's affordability push. A speech he gave last year had one section titled "Treasury Markets as a Barometer for Affordability."
  • Speaking to Axios, Bessent played down the signal from the recent yield surge, pointing out that borrowing costs have climbed around the world.
  • "I would be concerned if we were having some kind of idiosyncratic rise," he said. "It's been a global rise."

What to watch: The Treasury secretary recognized the limits of his influence on the bond market after this summer's intervention.

  • "I can't control the bond market," he said. "What I can do is try to get people to slow down and think."
  • Bessent said he does not regret declaring last month that "I am the house now," a reference to his informational advantage over Wall Street. "The house doesn't win every hand. The house plays percentages."

Go deeper: Watch the extended Scott Bessent interview on "The Axios Show"

item.title: The Iran war is hitting America's school buses — and kids are paying the price
item.description:
For millions of children, the school day starts on a diesel-powered bus with a driver behind the wheel. Now, school districts are struggling to afford both.

Why it matters: The Iran War is sending diesel costs higher just as districts are grappling with a yearslong bus driver shortage — a double whammy that can ripple into missed breakfasts, late classes and fewer school activities.

What they're saying: "We're a non-instructional expense for a district," Peter Mannella of the National Association for Pupil Transportation tells Axios.

  • "The inclination is always going to be let's see what we can cut out of transportation costs because we don't want to affect the school library," he says, adding that districts would rather protect spending on teachers, aides, and special education.

The big picture: Districts are consolidating routes, cutting trips and squeezing more efficiency out of their fleets.

  • A May survey of 188 school officials found 40% had adjusted routes, 27% enforced anti-idling rules, 25% cut routes, 20% limited optional trips, 14% changed fuel purchasing and 8% made students walk farther to stops.
  • Mannella said those changes result in more parents driving students to school activities or districts moving pickup points farther from students' homes.
  • "It starts to affect kids and families, which you know you'd rather not do," he said.

Case in point: Cherry Creek Public Schools outside Denver is short about 40 drivers, transportation director Mark Ingram tells Axios.

  • "It's an all hands on deck thing," he said. "Every morning and afternoon, we're looking at running some routes 10 to 15 minutes late … we just don't have the people to cover the routes."
  • For some students, that can mean missing the school-provided breakfast or arriving late to first period, he said.

Ingram's district has about 611 vehicles, including 320 yellow buses, plus vehicles for students with special needs and other district operations.

  • The district budgeted $1.5 million for fuel this year, up $300,000.
  • It now expects to spend roughly $2 million to $2.3 million. Ingram said the district hasn't cut services but is being frugal.

Zoom in: The driver shortage isn't just about wages.

  • Nick Martini, a former school bus driver who is now an executive at a Minneapolis-area school bus contractor, said drivers must simultaneously manage children and traffic while meeting extensive training, licensing and safety requirements.
  • Split shifts can keep drivers tied up for 10 to 12 hours while paying for only a fraction of that time, and districts compete with delivery and logistics companies for the same workers with commercial-driver's licenses.

Between the lines: Rural districts have even fewer escape routes.

  • Whereas kids in urban and suburban areas can sometimes walk to school, rural children may live miles from school, requiring longer bus routes, while districts struggle to match private-sector driver pay or hire third-party operators.
  • Special-needs transportation can be similarly expensive because curb-to-curb routes may have long gaps between stops.

Flashback: The Biden administration offered federal funding to electrify school bus fleets, but some of those programs have since slowed or ended, Association of School Business Officials International's Elleka Yost tells Axios.

  • Electric buses aren't an immediate fix everywhere. Yost pointed to narrow or winding roads, small bridges, extreme temperatures and a lack of trained technicians.

The bottom line: Districts will keep adapting, Mannella said.

  • "We are inherently problem solvers," he said. "Transportation is too important to just let us say, 'Well, we're not going to be able to do that anymore.' We'll find a way."

Go deeper: School bus tech drives classroom gains

item.title: Scoop: Trump's top national security aides meet secretly at Camp David on Iran, Yemen
item.description:
President Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Friday to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen, three U.S. officials told Axios.

Why it matters: The highly unusual meeting was not announced by the Trump administration. The last time a similar meeting took place was in June 2025, just days before Israel went to war against Iran.

The latest: Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed the Camp David meeting in a gaggle with reporters on Monday before heading to Europe.

  • "We constantly are meeting on long-term strategic planning and things of this nature. It is not unusual for us as a team to get together. That was just an opportunity to do it in a setting where there were less distractions," he said.
  • "That is part of the role the National Security Council plays — to bring together different stakeholders to do long-term planning. Six months, nine months, but in many cases five or 10 years down the road. I wouldn't call it routine ... but we had such meetings before," he added.

Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the officials said.

  • Among the other participants were Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, White House envoy Steve Witkoff, CIA director John Ratcliffe, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
  • "Things were decided or at least deeply discussed," one of the officials said, referring to the crisis in the Middle East.
  • The White House declined to comment.

Driving the news: With negotiations stalled, President Trump is considering resuming major combat operations in Iran.

  • "Now I have to make a decision: either Iran signs the deal, or it won't exist any longer," he said on Thursday.
  • At the same time, Trump is being asked to join Saudi Arabia's planned offensive against the Houthis in Yemen.
  • The Saudis are urging the president to conduct airstrikes against the Houthis. Trump has been leaning against it, but U.S. officials say he could change his mind.

What he's saying: On Friday afternoon, while his advisers were at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters what his next move on Iran will be.

  • "If I told you, you would have a major story," he said. "But you will see. It is working out very well. Iran is not doing well."

item.title: A Trump-sized shadow looms over the Supreme Court's new term
item.description:
The Supreme Court's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate-change litigation and gun control in their new term.

The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape.

  • The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed.

State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties.

  • On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December.
  • The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond.
  • While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation.

Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket.

  • Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status, enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship.

Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports.

  • The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements.
  • Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote.
  • More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term.

Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that.

  • After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks.
  • "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social.

In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did."

Go deeper: Trump's shadow docket blitz hits a new milestone

item.title: Strong data. Bad vibes. Voters are judging Trump's economy by prices.
item.description:
President Trump's economic data keeps getting stronger. His economic polling keeps getting worse by the day.

Why it matters: The midterms are less than a month away, and the administration is circling the drain on voters' No. 1 issue.

  • It may be too late to change that, but it's also not clear anyone has much of a plan to try.

What they're saying: "If I say 'oh, people are wrong, the economy is great,' then it looks like I'm insensitive. And if I then go into why the economy is great, then it looks like I'm insensitive," National Economic Council director Kevin Hassett said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union."

  • "It's true that the polls, which have gotten the president's success wrong every time, have been saying that people are looking a little bit depressed about the economy. But if you look at their actions, the actions speak way louder than words," Hassett added, citing spending and default data.

The big picture: There is ample evidence the economy is, statistically speaking, relatively strong.

  • 💰 Economic growth is solid and accelerating.
  • 💪 The labor market is relatively stable.
  • 💵 The K-shaped economy is ending as lower-end wages rise.
  • 🛍️ Public and private data say consumers are spending more than ever.

Yes, but: People feel lousy.

  • ☹️ The Conference Board's consumer confidence index is at a 12-year low.
  • 🐘 Republican sentiment in particular is eroding at its fastest rate since the Great Financial Crisis, per University of Michigan data.
  • 🪫 38% of voters told the latest CBS News poll their personal finances are fairly or very bad — a reflection, perhaps, of the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for months now. (When respondents were asked what they think about when they rate the economy, 91% said "prices.")
  • 👎 73% disapprove of President Trump's handling of the economy, per the latest AP-NORC survey, the lowest rating he — or President Biden — ever had. (69% say Trump's handling of cost-of-living issues has been worse than they expected in his second term.)

Friction point: When voters go to the polls, they don't bring the latest release from the Bureau of Economic Analysis with them.

  • They bring their feelings, and those are very bad.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told "The Axios Show" the administration wasn't going to repeat the Biden-era mistake of telling people how to feel.
  • But Trump himself said last week that Republicans weren't doing a good enough job of messaging.

The intrigue: So far, Trump's strategy seems to be the rich-uncle theory, which doesn't appear to be paying off with voters.

  • He continues to promise $5,000 checks for every adult citizen if Republicans win the midterms — a $1.3 trillion bombshell that most people don't believe he'll ever pay.
  • On Saturday, he promised seniors $2 billion in Medicare rebates, a big number that works out to about two weeks' worth of premium payments.

Between the lines: Some of the tension comes from the nature of the economic boom, an AI-fueled bonanza that nonetheless appears to be leaving many ordinary Americans behind.

  • It's not a K-shaped economy, says Krishna Guha, head of economics at Evercore ISI, but a "gator economy" — as in an alligator's mouth, where the bottom stays flat and the top is pointing to the sky poised to chomp.

The bottom line: There's good reason to think the economy's not that bad.

  • There's even better reason to think voters don't care.

Emily Peck contributed reporting.

item.title: Latino men swung hard to Trump in 2024. Now they're swinging back
item.description:
Latino voters, whose dramatic shift toward President Trump helped power his 2024 victory, are moving sharply back toward Democrats ahead of the midterms, two new national polls show.

Why it matters: Republicans built pieces of their 2026 strategy, including newly drawn House districts in Texas and Florida, around the assumption that Trump's historic Latino gains would endure. A reversal is complicating that bet in key races.

  • Trump's breakthrough with Latino men was among the clearest signs of a changing GOP coalition in 2024. Two years later, those gains look far less durable, though Democrats haven't recovered all the ground they lost in the last decade.

The latest: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll found Latino voters preferred Democratic control of Congress 59%–35% — a 24-point advantage, double the margin the same poll found in 2024.

  • A new CBS News/YouGov poll tells the same story: Hispanic likely voters favor Democratic House candidates 60%–39%.

Zoom in: Latino men have undergone a particularly strong political whiplash.

  • Hillary Clinton won Latino men by 31 points in 2016, according to the Edison National Election Pool exit poll, and Biden won them by 23 points in 2020. But in 2024, Trump won them by 10 points.
  • NBC now finds Latino men preferring Democratic congressional control 53%–39%.

Stunning stat: About one in seven Latino voters who say they backed Trump in 2024 now want Democrats to take control of Congress.

  • A majority of Latino voters say their congressional vote will be a signal against Trump.

Driving the shift: The economic squeeze felt by Latino voters hasn't changed much, but who they're blaming has.

  • Nearly two-thirds of Latino voters say their income is falling behind the cost of living in the NBC poll, almost exactly where that number stood in 2024. But 78% disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living.
  • Democrats now hold a 21-point advantage on handling the economy, after Trump held a 4-point edge over Harris in NBC's 2024 poll.
  • Trump's mass-deportation agenda has also sparked backlash: 67% say Trump's enforcement has gone too far.
  • The enforcement campaign has also become personal: 31% say they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported.

Yes, but: Polling voters a month before a midterm isn't the same as measuring who actually turns out.

  • Pew found that Trump's 2024 Hispanic gains were driven largely by changes in who voted that year, not by Biden voters switching to Trump.
  • In the NBC poll, 17% of voters said they or someone close to them was considering not voting in person because of fear of immigration enforcement.

Between the lines: Despite all this, Democrats haven't repaired their brand with Latino voters. Their net favorability has actually fallen by one point from 2024, but the GOP's has fallen by 18 points.

  • In 2016, 55% of Latino voters viewed the Democratic Party positively and 24% negatively — a 31-point net positive rating. Today, it's 41% positive and 42% negative.
  • Republicans have still made lasting inroads: Just 16% of Latino voters viewed the GOP positively in 2016, compared with 27% today. But negative views have also risen, from 57% then to 62% now.

What we're watching: Both parties are fighting over a large and growing Latino electorate in key races across Arizona, California, Florida and Texas.

item.title: App-makers are having a blast with the iPhone Duo, turning it into a retro Walkman
item.description:
The iPhone Duo isn't even out yet, but developers are already having fun with the new design, creating apps that turn Apple's first foldable smartphone into everything from an accordion to a retro Walkman.

Why it matters: Clever apps that couldn't exist on a traditional iPhone could help persuade early adopters to fork over nearly $2,000 for Apple's first foldable.

Flashback: It's reminiscent of the early days of the iPhone, when developers turned its giant touchscreen and sensors into virtual versions of familiar objects, such as the lighter apps with flames that flickered and swayed as the phone moved.

Zoom in: Among the apps is Duo-Man, a music player that turns the latest iPhone into a portable cassette player modeled on Sony's Walkman. Users open the Duo to choose an album and "insert" a cassette, then close it to start listening.

  • Even the clicks and static are actual recordings from a real Walkman.
  • It's the brainchild of indie app developer Vidit Bhargava, who created it during a four-hour hackathon late last month.
  • "I love the Walkman," he said. "I was just staring at it. I was like, this thing opens exactly like the iPhone Duo. What if your iPhone Duo was your Walkman, and you had to open up the door to change the album, and once you closed it, it would start playing the music?"
  • Bhargava has a particular affinity for the Walkman, having previously altered one of the vintage players to only work when a person is moving.

Zoom out: Developers are finding ways to make the fold itself part of the software. The San Francisco hackathon where Duo-Man was born produced 73 submitted Duo projects, ranging from games to music tools and a virtual pop-up book.

  • Accorduon turns the hinge into the bellows of a virtual accordion: The faster you fold and unfold the phone, the louder the instrument plays.
  • Crate, which took first place at the same hackathon where Duo-Man finished second, turns the Duo into a beat machine, where folding controls effects and snapping the phone open triggers a musical drop.
  • Foldtales uses the hinge to create a virtual pop-up book, with castles, trees and other objects rising as the phone opens.
  • Twofold uses the partially folded screen to hide each player's pieces in virtual versions of classic tabletop games.
  • And Delta developer Riley Testut is working on Duo support that could make the foldable iPhone resemble another familiar hinged gadget: Nintendo's dual-screen DS.

My thought bubble: Apple is years behind Samsung and Google in releasing a foldable phone. But its large developer ecosystem could help it catch up quick.

  • And the timing could turn out to be fortuitous. Developers are getting a new piece of hardware just as AI coding tools are making it faster and easier to turn a quirky idea into working software.

What we're watching: Whether the initial burst of experimentation produces enduring apps — and whether Apple sells enough Duos to reward developers for building custom apps.

item.title: Scoop: White House monitors suspected plague outbreak in Russia
item.description:
The White House is monitoring reports of a suspected plague case and related quarantines in Russia, a Trump administration official told Axios on Sunday.

Driving the news: Russian health authorities have taken precautionary measures in response to the death of a woman who worked at an anti-plague research facility, but have not confirmed that she contracted plague.

What they're saying: The Trump administration "is aware, monitoring the outbreak, and assessing options," the administration official said.

The backstory: On Sept. 25, 28-year-old Daria Shipilova, who worked at an anti-plague research institute in Russia's Irkutsk region, broke a test tube containing the pneumonic plague pathogen, local reports said.

  • Shipilova was admitted to a hospital on Sept. 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and died overnight between Oct. 1 and Oct. 2.
  • After her death, authorities imposed quarantines at several medical facilities in the region and placed nearly 200 people who had come into contact with Shipilova under medical observation.
  • Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said those being monitored showed no signs of illness and had tested negative.

Russian media reports suggested Shipilova may have contracted pneumonic plague, but health authorities have not confirmed the diagnosis.

  • Russia's public health agency said Shipilova had "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that further testing found no microorganisms linked to her work. The agency said the epidemiological situation in the region remains stable.

Zoom out: Plague is a potentially life-threatening bacterial disease but can be cured with antibiotics when treated promptly, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

White House spokespeople referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Iranian diplomats "kicked out" of U.S. after ignoring order to leave
item.description:
Two members of Iran's delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York were "kicked out" of the country on Saturday, several days after they were asked to leave, a U.S. official said.

  • "Secretary Rubio means business. Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in New York long after the UN General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the country," the official said.

Why it matters: It's the latest sign of tension between the two countries as diplomatic efforts to end the war falter and the prospect of renewed combat rises.

State of play: The U.S. official said the two Iranian diplomats did not obey a State Department demand to the Iranian mission to the UN on Monday that its entire delegation leave the country immediately.

  • On Friday, the Iranian mission to the UN was told the U.S. was aware the two diplomats were still in New York despite having asked them to leave. Iran was told again the two need to leave immediately.
  • One of the Iranian diplomats left on Friday night and the second on Saturday morning, the official said.

The other side: Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi disputed the U.S. account in a post on X Sunday.

  • "All Iranian diplomats who attended UNGA, except one who departed earlier, left as scheduled," he wrote. "Taking pride in fake diplomat "expulsion" is inappropriate for the head of any diplomatic corps. It oozes of desperation and defeat, and is inconsistent with UN host nation obligations."

item.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
item.description:
Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech.

  • "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said.

Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports.

  • When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy.
  • Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say.

Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia.

  • Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating.
  • The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets.
  • The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years.
  • The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco.

The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East.

  • U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said.
  • On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said.
  • A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems.

What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported.

  • It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

item.title: New York has a socialist mayor. Los Angeles may be next
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors.

Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries.

  • New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
  • The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3.
  • Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles.

State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020.

  • A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing.
  • A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided.

The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor.

  • It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters: Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided.

What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities.

  • Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India.
  • She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration.
  • "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment."

  • Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline.
  • She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement.

  • She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests.
  • Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people.
  • Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people."

Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one.
